beats.lead: The story people tell about AlphaZero is that it won chess by out-computing an old engine.
beats.text: DeepMind's own numbers say the opposite happened.
beats.note: It searched far less of the board, not more.

beats.name: AlphaZero
beats.role: DeepMind trained it on nothing but chess's rules and self-play — no opening books, no human games, no hand-built evaluation function.

beats.lead: It didn't take long to matter.
beats.text: Starting from random play, AlphaZero was already outplaying Stockfish, 2016's reigning world-champion engine, after 4 hours of training.
beats.note: 300,000 self-play steps, and it had already caught up.

beats.context: What AlphaZero actually searches per second in chess — against Stockfish's 70 million a second. It won by searching less, not more.

beats.lead: The final scoreline backs it up.
beats.text: A 100-game match at tournament time controls: 28 wins, 72 draws, 0 losses, for AlphaZero.
beats.note: Beaten on selectivity, not on speed.

beats.line: It won chess by thinking about less of it, more carefully.
